title: OIDC JAR / JARM — Signed Requests & Responses
subtitle: The authorization request is a signed JWT (JAR) and the authorization response comes back as a signed JWT (JARM) — integrity-protecting both legs against tampering and mix-up.

steps.label: Build & sign the request object
steps.lede: The client packs the authorization parameters — response_type, redirect_uri, scope, state, nonce, PKCE challenge, response_mode:jwt — into a JWT and signs it with its own key. This is the JAR request object.
steps.devtools: The header marks the JWT with typ: "oauth-authz-req+jwt". response_mode: "jwt" is what asks the AS to answer with a JARM response. The PKCE code_challenge travels inside the signed object, so it too is tamper-proof.

steps.label: GET /authorize?request=eyJ… (JAR by value)
steps.lede: The browser is sent to the authorization endpoint. Most parameters are gone from the query string — only client_id, response_type, and the big request JWT remain. (By reference, this would be a request_uri= instead.)
steps.devtools: In the Query String most params are missing — you see only client_id, response_type, and request=eyJ… (JAR by value) or request_uri=https://… (JAR by reference). Copy the request JWT, split on ., base64url-decode the payload to reveal the real redirect_uri, scope, state, nonce, and code_challenge.

steps.label: Verify request-object signature
steps.lede: The AS fetches the client's registered JWKS, verifies the request object's signature, and uses its claims as the authorization parameters. A tampered object is rejected with error=invalid_request_object.
steps.devtools: For JAR by reference the AS makes a server-to-server GET to the request_uri (e.g. https://client.example.com/req/abc123) to fetch the signed object — that fetch is not visible in the browser, only in a proxy capture. A bad signature surfaces later as a 302 …?error=invalid_request_object.

steps.label: Login + consent
steps.lede: The IdP authenticates the user (with MFA if required) and gathers consent. Credentials are entered against the IdP, never the client.
steps.devtools: You will see the IdP's own login HTML and an idp_session cookie set with HttpOnly; Secure. Verify the origin is the real IdP before entering credentials.

steps.label: 302 redirect with response=eyJ… (JARM)
steps.lede: Instead of a bare ?code=…&state=…, the IdP returns a single signed response JWT. Its claims — iss, aud, exp, code, state — are integrity-protected end to end.

jwt.title: Decoded JARM response JWT
payload: The AS that answered — MUST match the AS you sent to (mix-up defense)
Authorization code — trustworthy only after sig + iss/aud checks
Echoed CSRF token — must match what you sent

steps.devtools: In the Location header, instead of ?code=…&state=… you see one ?response=eyJ… JWT (or #response= for fragment.jwt, or a form POST for form_post.jwt). Decode the payload and check iss equals the AS you sent to and aud equals your client_id — then, and only then, trust the code.

steps.label: Verify JARM, extract code
steps.lede: The client verifies the response JWT's signature and checks iss and aud before touching the code. On an iss mismatch (a mix-up attempt) it discards the response and does NOT redeem the code.
steps.devtools: This is the mix-up defense in action: a response whose iss is not the expected AS — or whose signature fails — must be discarded. Never redeem a code from an unverified JARM response.

steps.label: POST /token — redeem the code
steps.lede: With the code verified, the client exchanges it at the token endpoint, sending the PKCE code_verifier. The AS returns an ID token and access token.

jwt.title: Decoded id_token
payload: Must equal the nonce in your request object — binds the id_token to this request

steps.devtools: Standard grant_type=authorization_code body with code_verifier. In the 200 response, decode the id_token and confirm its nonce matches the nonce you put in the request object — that ties the id_token back to this exact JAR request.
